blocks.text: Audio APIs cover two genuinely distinct directions, transcription converting speech to text, and text-to-speech converting written text into spoken audio, each with its own specific endpoint, parameters, and practical considerations.

This topic covers the transcription endpoint and supported audio formats, the text-to-speech endpoint with voice and speed settings, combining audio capability with text generation into a pipeline, and practical considerations for using audio at real scale.
1. Two Directions, Speech to Text and Text to Speech

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Building on image generation, audio APIs cover two directions

blocks.text: Audio capability splits into two genuinely distinct directions, converting spoken audio into written text, transcription, and converting written text into spoken audio, text-to-speech, each solving a different problem with its own dedicated endpoint.

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Speech to text handles transcription, text to speech handles voice synthesis

blocks.text: 2. The Transcription Endpoint

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: An audio file uploaded goes to the transcription endpoint, returning a text transcript

blocks.text: The transcription endpoint accepts an audio file and returns the spoken content as written text, this connects directly to the request body concepts covered in an earlier module, though here the payload is audio data rather than a JSON messages array.

code.content:
with open("meeting_recording.mp3", "rb") as audio_file:
    transcript = client.audio.transcriptions.create(
        model="whisper-1", file=audio_file,
    )
print(transcript.text)

blocks.text: 3. Supported Formats and Size Limits

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Supported formats include mp3 and wav, with a file size limit applying

blocks.text: Transcription endpoints typically support several common audio formats, and enforce a maximum file size, a genuinely long recording may need to be split into smaller segments before transcription, checking the specific provider documentation for the exact limit avoids an unexpected rejection.

blocks.text: 4. The Text-to-Speech Endpoint

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Text input provided goes to the text-to-speech endpoint, returning an audio file

blocks.text: The text-to-speech endpoint accepts written text and returns generated spoken audio, the reverse direction of transcription, useful for reading content aloud, generating voice responses for a voice assistant, or producing narrated content.

code.content:
response = client.audio.speech.create(
    model="tts-1", voice="alloy", input="Welcome to the application.",
)
response.stream_to_file("welcome.mp3")

blocks.text: 5. Voice Selection and Speed

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A voice option and a speed setting control the generated speech

blocks.text: Text-to-speech endpoints typically offer several distinct voice options to choose from, and a speed setting controlling how quickly the generated speech plays, matching these settings to your actual application, a customer facing assistant versus an accessibility reading tool, shapes the resulting user experience meaningfully.

blocks.title: Voice choice is a genuine product decision, not just a technical setting
blocks.content: The specific voice selected shapes how users perceive an application personality, exactly connecting to the persona design concepts covered in an earlier module, worth choosing deliberately rather than defaulting arbitrarily.

blocks.text: 6. Real-Time vs Batch Audio Processing

Some audio use cases need near real-time processing, a live voice conversation, others work fine with batch processing, transcribing a large backlog of recorded meetings overnight, this distinction shapes whether streaming, covered in an earlier module, or simple batch calls better fit your specific application.
7. Combining Audio With Text Generation

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Transcribing then summarizing with a chat model forms a combined pipeline

blocks.text: This connects directly to prompt chaining, covered in an earlier module, a common, genuinely useful pipeline transcribes an audio recording first, then feeds that transcript into a standard chat completion call for summarization, question answering, or further analysis, combining audio and text capability into one coherent workflow.
8. A Worked Audio Pipeline Example

A meeting notes application transcribes an uploaded recording, then passes the resulting transcript through a chat completion call with a system prompt instructing it to extract action items and key decisions, combining both audio capabilities and the prompt engineering techniques covered throughout this course into one complete feature.
9. Practical Scale Considerations

Audio processing at real volume carries its own cost and time considerations, transcribing a large batch of long recordings takes real processing time and cost, planning for this, exactly the cost tracking discipline covered in an earlier module applied here to audio, matters for any application processing audio at scale.
Worked Example

A customer support team building a call summary feature initially processes each support call recording as one single, very long transcription request, occasionally hitting the file size limit on their longest calls and failing entirely.

Splitting longer recordings into smaller segments before transcription, then combining the resulting transcript segments before passing them to a summarization step, resolves this limit issue entirely, letting the feature handle calls of any length reliably.
Common Mistakes

items: Not checking the file size limit before attempting to transcribe a genuinely long audio recording
Choosing a voice for text-to-speech arbitrarily rather than deliberately matching it to the application persona
Not accounting for the real time and cost audio processing takes at genuine volume
Missing the opportunity to combine transcription with a text generation step for a more complete pipeline

blocks.text: Practice

Sketch out a pipeline combining transcription and a chat completion call for a task you are familiar with, meeting notes, customer call analysis, or a voice memo summarizer, specifying what the system prompt for the summarization step should actually instruct.
Key Takeaway

Audio APIs cover two distinct directions, transcription converting speech to text and text-to-speech converting text to spoken audio, each with its own endpoint, format and size considerations, and voice or speed settings, and combining transcription with a standard chat completion call is a genuinely powerful pattern for building a complete audio-aware application feature.
